procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Judicature at Bombay
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 22.02.1999-25.02.1999 of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in Criminal Writ Petition No.1146 of 1997.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Criminal Writ Petition No. 1146 of 1997 was heard and a judgment/order was issued on 22.02.1999-25.02.1999.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Criminal Appeal No. 1255 of 1999 was filed in the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's judgment/order. Other related cases were also before the court: Criminal Appeal Nos.1256, 1367 of 1999, Contempt Petition (Civil) No.47 of 2011 In Writ Petition (C) No.316 Of 2008, Tc (C) No.27 of 2011 And Writ Petition (Civil) No.316 Of 2008

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Every accused person is entitled to the presumption of innocence during the investigation and trial stages. Media reporting that implicates the culpability of an individual under investigation can seriously infringe upon their reputation and personal dignity.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court finds that a balance must be maintained between the media's fundamental right to free speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a), which includes the public's right to be informed about criminal investigations, and the accused's fundamental right to life and personal liberty under Article 21, which encompasses the right to a fair and unbiased investigation and the presumption of innocence. This balancing is particularly crucial during the pre-trial stage, where unfair media reporting has the potential to affect public opinion and impinge upon the accused's rights.
legal_tests_applied: Balancing of fundamental rights, specifically the right to free speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) against the right to life and personal liberty (including fair trial and presumption of innocence) under Article 21.
policy_considerations: The primary concern of the police ought to be the fair administration of justice without compromising on individual rights of privacy or of presumption of innocence.
Media reporting on crimes involves significant elements of public interest, bearing upon the right to be informed and the right to know.
Unfair reporting by the media has the potential to affect public opinion and impinge upon the presumption of innocence, which is a cardinal principle.
The rights of the accused and of the victims or survivors of crimes have a direct bearing on the fundamental right to life and personal liberty.
Information ought not to be released by the police which would portray them as insensitive or vindictive or which would suggest the pre-judging of an issue.

Any disclosure by the police about an investigation must be cognizant of the fact that the information as disclosed impacts not only upon the victim of the crime and the accused, but on the rule of law.
